hmmt-feb-2020-geo-01.title: Solution
hmmt-feb-2020-geo-01.body:
$DIAL$ is a square with side $ID=1$ (so $LA=1$), $FRIEND$ is a regular hexagon with side $1$ (sharing the side $ID$ with the square) and $FOR$ is an equilateral triangle on its side $FR$.

Focusing on $FRIEND$ and $FOR$ first: either $DIO$ is an equilateral triangle, or $O$ is the midpoint of $ID$ (depending on which side of $FR$ the triangle is drawn). In every case $OLA$ is an isosceles triangle with base $LA=1$, and the possible distances from $O$ to the line $LA$ are $1$, $1-\frac{\sqrt3}2$ and $1+\frac{\sqrt3}2$ (here $\frac{\sqrt3}2$ is the distance from $O$ to $ID$ in the equilateral case). The corresponding areas are $\frac12$, $\frac12\left(1-\frac{\sqrt3}2\right)$, $\frac12\left(1+\frac{\sqrt3}2\right)$, with product $$\frac18\left(1-\frac34\right)=\frac1{32}.$$

**Answer: $\frac1{32}$**

hmmt-feb-2020-geo-02.title: Solution
hmmt-feb-2020-geo-02.body:
Let the side length be $s$. In the regular hexagon, the diagonal $WZ=2s$ is parallel to the side $UV$, which lies on $AB$, so $WZ\parallel AB$ and triangles $WCZ$ and $ACB$ are similar. Also in triangle $AVW$ we have $\angle A=60^\circ$ and $\angle AVW=180^\circ-120^\circ=60^\circ$ (the hexagon's interior angle at $V$ is $120^\circ$), so $AVW$ is equilateral with $AW=VW=s$. Then $WC=8-s$ and $\frac{WC}{WZ}=\frac{AC}{AB}$ gives $\frac{8-s}{2s}=\frac85$, i.e. $5(8-s)=16s$, so $s=\frac{40}{21}$.

**Answer: $\frac{40}{21}$**

hmmt-feb-2020-geo-03.title: Solution
hmmt-feb-2020-geo-03.body:
Place the tromino with a tall column $[0,1]\times[0,2]$ and a foot $[1,2]\times[0,1]$ (total area $3$). The segment $AB$ must cut off area $\frac32$. The tromino is symmetric in the line $y=x$, so we may assume an endpoint $A=(x,0)$ lies on the bottom edge and the other endpoint $B$ lies above the line $x+y=\sqrt3$ or on the left side as described below (the remaining cases are reflections).

For $A$ from $(0,0)$ to $(1.5,0)$, the other endpoint $B$ moves along the boundary from $(1,1)$ through $(1,2)$ to $(0,2)$; all these segments lie in the rectangle $0\le x\le1.5$, $0\le y\le2$, whose diagonal is $\sqrt{2^2+1.5^2}=\frac52$, attained at $A=(1.5,0)$, $B=(0,2)$ (the segment cuts off a triangle of area $\frac12\cdot1.5\cdot2=\frac32$). For $A=(x,0)$ with $1.5\le x\le\sqrt3$, $B=(0,\frac3x)$ and the length is $\sqrt{x^2+\frac9{x^2}}$, which is largest at the endpoint $x=1.5$ (the farther $x^2$ is from $3$ the larger $x^2+9/x^2$), giving $\frac52$ again. So the maximum is $\frac52$.

**Answer: $\frac52$**

hmmt-feb-2020-geo-04.title: Solution
hmmt-feb-2020-geo-04.body:
Let $\omega_1$ touch $AD$, $BC$ at $R$, $S$ and $\omega_2$ touch $AD$, $AB$ at $X$, $Y$. Let $r=AX=AY$ be the inradius of right triangle $ABE$ (right angle at $A$, so $AXOY$ is a square), $a=EX=ET=ER$ and $b=BY=BT=BS$. Since $RS\parallel CD$, $ABSR$ is a rectangle with $RS=AB$, and $AR=BS$ gives $r+2a=b$ ($AR=AX+XE+ER=r+2a$). Then $AE=a+r$, $AB=b+r=2(a+r)$, and $BE=(a+r)\sqrt5$. On the other hand $BE=BT+TE=b+a=r+3a$. So $(a+r)\sqrt5=r+3a$, giving $a=\frac{1+\sqrt5}{2}r$. The radius of $\omega_1$ is $\frac12RS=\frac12AB=a+r$, so the ratio is $\frac{a+r}{r}=\frac{3+\sqrt5}{2}$.

**Answer: $\frac{3+\sqrt5}{2}$**

hmmt-feb-2020-geo-05.title: Solution
hmmt-feb-2020-geo-05.body:
Rotate the region $BCDE\setminus\text{disk}$ about $A$ by multiples of $60^\circ$: rotating quadrilateral $BCDE$ about $A$ six times gives a larger regular hexagon of side $4$ (area $\frac{3\sqrt3}2\cdot16=24\sqrt3$) with $A$ at its center, and the disk of radius $3$ about $A$ lies inside it (the inradius of the large hexagon is $2\sqrt3>3$). So the six copies of the desired region have total area $24\sqrt3-9\pi$, and the desired area is $\frac16(24\sqrt3-9\pi)=4\sqrt3-\frac32\pi$.

**Answer: $4\sqrt3-\frac{3}{2}\pi$**

hmmt-feb-2020-geo-06.title: Solution
hmmt-feb-2020-geo-06.body:
Let the incircle with center $I$ and radius $r$ touch $AB,BC,CA$ at $X,Y,Z$. The tangent lengths are $BX=BY=2$, $CY=CZ=4$, $AZ=AX=3$ (semiperimeter $s=9$). Then $XD=XB+BD=2+7=9$, $YE=YC+CE=4+5=9$, $ZF=ZA+AF=3+6=9$. The right triangles $IXD$, $IYE$, $IZF$ have legs $r$ and $9$, so $ID=IE=IF$, i.e. $I$ is the circumcenter of $DEF$.

By Heron, $[ABC]=\sqrt{9\cdot4\cdot3\cdot2}=6\sqrt6$, so $r=\frac{6\sqrt6}9=\frac{2\sqrt6}3$. The circumradius satisfies $ID^2=r^2+9^2=\frac{8}{3}+81=\frac{251}3$, so the area is $\frac{251}3\pi$.

**Answer: $\frac{251\pi}{3}$**

hmmt-feb-2020-geo-07.title: Solution
hmmt-feb-2020-geo-07.body:
Let $O,O_1,O_2$ be the centers, $r_1=2$, $r_2=3$, $R=12$, and let $d$ be the signed distance from $O$ to $AB$ (positive if $O$ and $O_1$ are on the same side of $AB$; the circles $\omega_1,\omega_2$ lie on opposite sides of the internal tangent). Then $OO_i=R-r_i$, and $\cos\angle T_1O_1O=\frac{r_1-d}{R-r_1}$, $\cos\angle T_2O_2O=\frac{r_2+d}{R-r_2}$. Since $X_1,O_1,O$ are collinear with $X_1$ beyond $O_1$, $\angle X_1O_1T_1=180^\circ-\angle T_1O_1O$, so
$$X_1T_1=r_1\sqrt{2+2\cos\angle T_1O_1O}=r_1\sqrt{2\,\frac{R-d}{R-r_1}},\qquad X_2T_2=r_2\sqrt{2\,\frac{R+d}{R-r_2}}.$$ The condition $4X_1T_1^2=X_2T_2^2$ gives $8r_1^2\frac{R-d}{R-r_1}=2r_2^2\frac{R+d}{R-r_2}$, i.e. $\frac{32(12-d)}{10}=\frac{18(12+d)}{9}=2(12+d)$. So $3.2(12-d)=2(12+d)$, $d=\frac{36}{13}$. Hence $AB=2\sqrt{R^2-d^2}=2\sqrt{144-\frac{1296}{169}}=\frac{96\sqrt{10}}{13}$.

**Answer: $\frac{96\sqrt{10}}{13}$**

hmmt-feb-2020-geo-08.title: Solution
hmmt-feb-2020-geo-08.body:
Let $H_a$ be the foot of the altitude from $A$ to $BC$. Since $AE$ bisects $\angle H_aAV$ (the altitude and the circumdiameter are isogonal), the angle bisector theorem in triangle $AH_aV$ gives $\frac{AH_a}{H_aE}=\frac{AV}{VE}$. The right triangles $AH_aE$ and $ANA'$ are similar ($\angle ANA'=90^\circ$ as $AA'$ is a diameter), so $\frac{AN}{NA'}=\frac{AH_a}{H_aE}$.

Let $R$ be the radius: $AA'=2R$, $AN=\sqrt{4R^2-81}$, $AV=2R-7$. Then $$\frac{\sqrt{4R^2-81}}{9}=\frac{2R-7}{6}\ \Rightarrow\ 9(2R-7)^2=4(4R^2-81)\ \Rightarrow\ 20R^2-252R+765=0,$$ i.e. $(2R-15)(10R-51)=0$. The triangle is acute so $VA'<R$, so $VA'=7<R$ rules out $R=\frac{51}{10}$. So $R=\frac{15}2$.

**Answer: $\frac{15}{2}$**

hmmt-feb-2020-geo-09.title: Solution
hmmt-feb-2020-geo-09.body:
Let $r_a,r_b,r_c$ be the radii and $k_i=1/r_i$ the curvatures. $DEF$ is the contact triangle of $ABC$ and $AD,BE,CF$ concur at the Gergonne point $T$, whose barycentric coordinates with respect to $ABC$ are proportional to $\frac1{r_a}:\frac1{r_b}:\frac1{r_c}$ (the tangent lengths from $A,B,C$ to the incircle are $r_b+r_c-\dots$; indeed $AF=r_a$ etc., so the Gergonne point is $(\frac1{s-a}:\frac1{s-b}:\frac1{s-c})=(\frac1{r_a}:\frac1{r_b}:\frac1{r_c})$).

The distance from $T$ to the common tangent line $\ell$ is the weighted average of the distances from $A,B,C$ to $\ell$, which are $r_a,r_b,r_c$ (all three circles lie on one side of $\ell$). So $$d=\frac{\frac1{r_a}r_a+\frac1{r_b}r_b+\frac1{r_c}r_c}{\frac1{r_a}+\frac1{r_b}+\frac1{r_c}}=\frac{3}{k_a+k_b+k_c}.$$ The line $\ell$ is a circle of curvature $0$ tangent to all three, and the other tangent circle has radius $49$. Descartes' theorem gives $k_a+k_b+k_c+2\sqrt{k_ak_b+k_bk_c+k_ck_a}=\frac1{49}$ and $k_a+k_b+k_c-2\sqrt{k_ak_b+k_bk_c+k_ck_a}=0$. Adding, $k_a+k_b+k_c=\frac1{98}$, so $d=3\cdot98=294$. (The radius $341$ is not needed.)

**Answer: 294**

hmmt-feb-2020-geo-10.title: Solution
hmmt-feb-2020-geo-10.body:
Fix $P$ with $OP=x$ and consider friendly circles $\Omega$ centered at $P$. Invert about a point on ray $OP$ chosen so that $\Gamma$ and $\Omega$ become concentric; the chain $\omega_1,\dots,\omega_{2020}$ is preserved, and for concentric circles the radius ratio must be one of finitely many values (determined by $\theta=\frac{\pi k}{2020}$, $\gcd(k,2020)=1$). Carrying the inversion out, the radius $\rho$ of $\Omega$ satisfies a quadratic in $\rho$ whose two roots $\rho_1,\rho_2$ (for each admissible $k$ and $x$) are swapped by the inversion about $P$ with radius $\sqrt{1-x^2}$, so $\rho_1\rho_2=1-x^2$, while $\rho_1+\rho_2$ equals the same value as for $x=0$ (it does not depend on $x$).

The admissible values of $k$ with $k<1010$ give $\frac{\varphi(2020)}2=400$ pairs. For each pair the total area of the two circles is $\pi(\rho_1^2+\rho_2^2)=\pi\left((\rho_1+\rho_2)^2-2\rho_1\rho_2\right)$, so the pair's contribution to $f(A)-f(B)$ is $2\pi\left(OA^2-OB^2\right)=2\pi\left(\frac14-\frac19\right)=\frac{5\pi}{18}$. Therefore $f(A)-f(B)=400\cdot\frac{5\pi}{18}=\frac{1000\pi}9$.

**Answer: $\frac{1000\pi}{9}$**
